source.title: Efficient Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Molecular Graph Transformer Models
source.authors: Yi-Li Wang; Kai-ya Zhou; Ning-Hao Liu; Ying Wang; Xin Wang

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether sharpness-aware optimization and a loss-landscape measure relate to generalization, using molecular graph transformers and molecular-property benchmarks rather than the claim versions’ specified methods and settings.
record.gate_note: The paper compares test metrics for Adam, SAM, and GraphSAM and describes their loss landscapes. It does not test random-label memorization, width, image convolutions versus fully connected networks, adaptive optimizers versus SGD, batch size, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness measures, or removal of influential training examples.
record.test_reason: The study uses the sharpness–generalization rationale to develop and evaluate GraphSAM. Its optimizer comparisons and unscaled loss-landscape visualizations do not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness–gap relationship. Adam is the base optimizer for both molecular backbones, so comparisons with SAM variants also do not test V4's adaptive-versus-SGD claim. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that pretraining-free graph transformers encounter sharp minima, that SAM improves their generalization, and that GraphSAM retains comparable predictive performance with higher throughput. The illustrated Adam train–test loss gap is correctly reported. These conclusions do not establish V7's magnitude-aware sharpness relationship.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAM and a proposed approximation, GraphSAM, on molecular graph property prediction; it does not reproduce the listed claim-version methods or datasets.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and model affect the reported test metrics. The paper also reports effects from the perturbation radius and its schedule, and from how often GraphSAM re-anchors its perturbation gradient.

fits_no_version.finding: In Table 1, SAM and GraphSAM improve every reported mean test metric over Adam for both molecular graph transformer backbones. These are optimizer-performance comparisons; training performance is not reported alongside them.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM and GraphSAM can improve held-out molecular-property prediction over Adam for the tested pretraining-free GROVER and CoMPT recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: The BBBP GROVER visualization shows a sharper Gaussian-direction loss landscape for Adam than SAM or GraphSAM. The authors describe a large Adam training–testing loss gap and rank test loss as SAM best, GraphSAM second, Adam worst in Figure 5, which includes both backbones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the illustrated molecular-transformer experiments, sharpness-aware optimization accompanies flatter unscaled loss profiles and better held-out loss than Adam.

record.problems: The paper does not report training-error values alongside the Table 1 test metrics, so those comparisons do not establish training–test gap changes. The loss-landscape and loss-curve descriptions are qualitative; their plotted values are not given in the text. The paper's sharpness comparisons are not magnitude-aware measures. Table 1 reports means and standard deviations across five-fold cross-validation and five replicated experiments per task.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded optimizer throughput results, additional BACE/QM7/QM8 results, hyperparameter sweeps, and attention entropy: these do not directly measure the claim's listed conditions or magnitude-aware sharpness/generalization-gap relation. Reported in Tables 2–10 and Figures 6–10.

untested.parts: Fixed random-label fitting versus natural-label fitting and their held-out accuracy under the same architecture and recipe.
Width increases beyond zero training error and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD under limited or broader tuning; switching optimizers and decoupled weight decay.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations that change the large-batch penalty.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, underfitting, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.

Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance versus train–test error gaps among similarly low-training-loss networks, and ranking against norm- and margin-based measures. Gaussian-direction landscape plots, test metrics, and a discussion citing scale dependence do not test these quantities.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All Table 1 numbers match the supplied text. Rows describing optimizer performance belong under fits_no_version rather than serving as claim evidence. Changing their states to cannot_determine does not deny the reported improvements; no listed version's effect can be inferred from those measures. The scale-dependence discussion cites prior work and supplies no independent test of magnitude-aware sharpness. Table 11 compares SGD with SAM variants on images, not adaptive optimizers with SGD, so it does not supply missing V4 evidence.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers compared with SGD under different tuning regimes.
Magnitude-scaled weight perturbations, comparisons against norm- and margin-based measures, and gap ranking among similarly low-training-loss networks.
Removing memorized training examples and retraining.
